## About 10.6x, from 64 cores

Amdahl's law, with `s` the serial fraction and `N` the cores:

```
speedup = 1 / (s + (1 - s)/N)
        = 1 / (0.08 + 0.92/64)
        = 1 / (0.08 + 0.014375)
        = 1 / 0.094375
        = 10.6
```

So 64 cores bought you **10.6x**, an efficiency of 10.6/64 = **17%**. Eighty-three per cent of the machine is idle, waiting.

## The number worth memorising is the ceiling

Let `N` go to infinity and the parallel term vanishes:

```
max speedup = 1 / s = 1 / 0.08 = 12.5x
```

**An infinite number of cores gets you 12.5x.** You already have 10.6 of that 12.5 from 64 cores — 85% of the theoretical maximum, with nothing left to buy. That is the real content of the law: not the figure for 64 cores, but that the figure barely moves afterwards.

| Cores | Speedup | Efficiency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1.0x | 100% |
| 8 | 5.0x | 63% |
| 32 | 8.8x | 28% |
| 64 | 10.6x | 17% |
| 256 | 11.9x | 5% |
| infinite | 12.5x | 0% |

Going from 64 cores to 256 — four times the hardware — gains 12%. Going from 8 to 64, eight times the hardware, barely doubles it.

## What to do instead

The table says the serial fraction is the only lever that matters, and that is the practical lesson. Cut the serial part from 8% to 2%:

```
ceiling       = 1/0.02 = 50x
at 64 cores   = 1/(0.02 + 0.92/64 + 0.06/64) ~ 29x
```

Nearly three times the speedup at the same core count, from optimising the part that **does not run in parallel**. Shaving the parallel section is almost worthless by comparison — it is already divided by 64.

So the order of work is: profile, find the serial fraction, attack *that*, and only then think about cores. Teams routinely do this backwards, parallelise the hot loop, measure 10x on a 64-core box and conclude the machine is the problem.

## Two honest caveats

**This is an optimistic bound.** It assumes the parallel part divides perfectly with zero communication, zero synchronisation and perfect load balance. Real code also pays for thread creation, locks, cache-line ping-pong and memory bandwidth contention, all of which *grow* with `N`. Measured curves usually peak and then decline. Amdahl gives the best case and you will not reach it.

**Gustafson's law is the other half.** Amdahl asks "how much faster is this fixed problem?" Gustafson asks "how much bigger a problem can I do in the same time?" — and for a lot of scientific computing the second is the real question, because the serial part (setup, I/O) stays roughly constant while the parallel part grows with the problem size. Weak scaling looks far better than strong scaling, and that is not a trick: it is a different question with a different answer.
